opus-5.5.text:
Well, I think one of the most interesting things is that we've actually come at this question backwards for a long time. Philosophers of science, people like Kuhn and the Bayesians and so on, have been asking how it is that scientists can take the data that comes in from the world and come up with these abstract, structured theories that go way beyond that data. And that's a genuinely deep puzzle. It's the old problem of induction: how do you get from the photons hitting your retina, or the numbers on a spreadsheet, to quarks and evolution and the structure of DNA?

What I've argued, starting back in the eighties and nineties with what we called the "theory theory," is that the best place to look for an answer isn't actually in the lab or the history of science. It's in the nursery. Babies and young children solve exactly that same problem, and they do it faster and more effectively than any scientist. In the first few years of life, children work out an intuitive physics, an intuitive biology, and especially an intuitive psychology, a theory of other people's minds. And they do it the way scientists do: they make predictions, they notice when those predictions go wrong, they revise. They even experiment. What looks like a two-year-old just getting into everything is actually something much more like systematic exploration.

So the picture I'd give is that science isn't some special cultural invention that sits on top of ordinary cognition. It's more that science takes these very powerful learning capacities that we all have as children and puts them to work in a more institutional, cumulative way. Scientists have advantages: they have instruments, they have mathematics, and above all they have a whole community that checks each other's work. But the basic engine is the same one that children are using.

And in the last couple of decades we've been able to say something more precise about what that engine is. A lot of it looks like a kind of probabilistic, Bayesian inference over structured models, especially causal models. You have a set of hypotheses about how the world works, each with some probability, and as evidence comes in, you shift those probabilities around. What's striking is that in experiments, even preschoolers do this in a pretty sophisticated way. If you show them statistical patterns of evidence about which blocks make a machine light up, they'll infer the right causal structure, and they'll intervene in the right way to test it.

The piece I've become more and more interested in is what you might call the explore-exploit tradeoff. There's a real tension in any learning system between exploiting what you already know to act effectively, and exploring, trying things that are low-probability, maybe a bit crazy, just to find out. Children are designed to be explorers. They have this long protected period of childhood where they don't have to worry about getting things done, and that lets them try out weird hypotheses. And I think good science depends on preserving some of that childlike willingness to entertain the improbable idea. The scientific institutions that work best are the ones that create a kind of protected space, a bit like childhood, where people can explore without immediately having to pay off.

fable-5.1.text:
Well, I think the first thing to say is that it's not as different from how children learn about the world as people tend to assume. That's really been the central theme of my work. When you look at what a four-year-old does — she has a kind of theory about how the world works, she makes predictions on the basis of that theory, she goes out and does what we'd call experiments, though she'd just call it playing — and when the predictions don't come out right, she revises the theory. That's a pretty good description of what scientists do, too.

The big difference isn't so much in the underlying process as in the social and institutional scaffolding. Scientists have journals and peer review and grant committees and conferences, which are, in a way, just very elaborate mechanisms for doing what a child does naturally — taking in evidence from other people, checking what you believe against what someone else believes, and updating. And of course, scientists have mathematics and instruments that let them get at evidence a child couldn't get at.

But I'd actually push a little further and say that in some respects children are better at it. One of the things we've found is that young children are more willing to consider unlikely hypotheses. If you give adults a problem where the obvious answer doesn't work, they'll keep trying variations on the obvious answer. Four-year-olds will go to the weird answer much faster. There's a kind of exploration-exploitation trade-off here. Children are at the explore end of the spectrum — their whole job is to figure out what the world is like, not to do anything in particular with that knowledge. Adults, including adult scientists, are under pressure to exploit, to use what they already know to get things done. So the ideal scientist is probably someone who has managed to keep a bit of that childlike willingness to be wrong and to look in strange places, while also having the discipline and the tools that come with being an adult.

And I'd add one more thing, which is that I think a lot of what we call scientific learning is really Bayesian in character — you're not just confirming or disconfirming theories one at a time, you've got a whole distribution of possibilities and the evidence shifts your confidence across that distribution. We've found that even very young children seem to be doing something like that. So the picture of science as this special, almost unnatural human activity — I think that's wrong. It's a formalized, amplified version of something that's deeply part of what it is to be a human being, and it shows up most clearly, and most charmingly, in very small children.

astra-6.text:
I think a useful way to understand it is to start with how children learn. We tend to think of science as this very specialized activity, which, of course, it is. But some of its basic capacities—the ability to imagine ways the world could be, to test those possibilities, and to change your mind in light of evidence—are capacities you can see even in very young children.

The interesting problem is that all we ever get is a particular collection of experiences, and yet we somehow work out something about the structure of the world that produced those experiences. We don’t just record what happened. We construct explanations. And those explanations let us make predictions, but they also let us say, “What would happen if I did something differently?”

Experiment is especially important because intervening in the world gives you information that simply observing it doesn’t. A child trying the same thing several different ways and a scientist designing an experiment are both exploiting that fact.

What science adds is a set of social practices that makes this process much more effective. We can make our ideas explicit, share evidence, criticize one another’s explanations, and accumulate discoveries across generations. So I’d see science as building on very basic human learning abilities, with institutions that extend those abilities and help correct their mistakes.

sol-6.1.text:
I think scientists learn in much the same way that children do. They start out with some picture of how the world works, and then they explore, try things out, and see whether what happens fits that picture. When it doesn’t, they have to consider other possibilities.

What’s remarkable is that we can move beyond the particular things we’ve observed to understand something about the underlying causal structure of the world. We don’t just learn that two things go together. We try to figure out whether changing one would change the other. Experiments are especially powerful because they let us distinguish between explanations that might otherwise look equally plausible.

Science takes those basic capacities for exploration and learning and gives them a social structure. We can criticize one another’s ideas, accumulate evidence across generations, and devise instruments that let us discover things our ordinary experience would never reveal.
